strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple algorithms (FastTD3, FastSAC, PPO) and diverse benchmarks (HumanoidBench, IsaacGym, Atari, MTBench, offline-to-online RL)
Clear problem motivation with well-framed analysis connecting non-stationarity to representation collapse, supported by CIFAR-10 toy experiment and formal analysis

Multi-faceted mechanistic analysis beyond returns: effective rank, dormant neurons, gradient stability, TD error, critic disagreement, Cramér distance, and sparsity metrics that strengthen causal claims
Practical simplicity: lightweight architectural modification requiring no auxiliary losses with negligible computational overhead (~5-10% wall-clock), making it readily adoptable
Consistent improvements across diverse settings and algorithms, demonstrating broad applicability
Extensive ablation studies on key hyperparameters (L, V) and design choices (CDQ, C51, noise scaling) with robust results across variants
Real robot validation (Booster T1) adds practical relevance beyond simulation
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, architecture specifications, and comprehensive per-environment learning curves in appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is applying existing SEM technique (Lavoie et al., 2023) to RL without algorithmic modifications to RL methods themselves; primarily an application paper rather than methodological contribution

Modest empirical improvements (typically 10-25% sample efficiency gains) with incomplete statistical rigor: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance analysis reported; Atari uses only 3 seeds vs. 6 for continuous control

Incomplete hyperparameter understanding: introduces three hyperparameters (L, V, τ) but provides limited guidance for practitioners; ablations restricted to 5 HumanoidBench tasks due to computational constraints, limiting generalizability of findings

Weak theoretical justification: Theorem 1 is relatively straightforward (non-stationarity increases dormancy); connection between 'energy preservation' and collapse prevention is intuitive but not rigorously established; no convergence guarantees specific to RL setting

Limited experimental scope: primarily continuous control, small Atari subset (10 games), no vision-based continuous control experiments; comparison with discrete representation methods (Gumbel-ST, VQ, C-RELU) restricted to single figure
Artificial CIFAR-10 experiment with discrete label shuffling as poor proxy for continuous RL non-stationarity from evolving policies; weak connection to actual dynamics

Incomplete failure analysis: no clear characterization of when SEM fails or provides minimal benefit; missing systematic sensitivity analysis for temperature parameter τ; no ablations explaining why improvements are marginal on some tasks

Presentation issues: dense figures with many subplots difficult to parse; connection between formal analysis (Appendix B) and main claims unclear; lack of visualization of learned representations (e.g., dimensionality reduction)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple algorithms (FastTD3, FastTD3-SimBaV2, FastSAC, PPO) and diverse benchmarks (HumanoidBench, IsaacGym, Atari, MTBench, real robot)
Extensive representation-level analysis with diagnostic metrics (effective rank, dormant neurons, Gini sparsity, Cramér distance, entropy) providing mechanistic insights
Well-written paper with clear motivation and thorough appendices supporting reproducibility details
Minimal computational overhead with no wall-clock slowdown (Table 2), making the approach practical
Systematic ablation studies examining hyperparameter sensitivity (L, V, τ) and design choices across different settings
weaknesses: Limited novelty: SEM is from prior work (Lavoie et al., 2023); core contribution is empirical application to RL without new insights into why SEM helps

Weak theoretical justification: CIFAR-10 label-shuffling experiment is an artificial proxy for RL non-stationarity; Theorem 1 uses standard SGD analysis to show non-stationarity increases dormancy but doesn't explain why group-wise softmax specifically solves this

Modest and variable empirical improvements: many gains are 10-20% with high task variance; improvements often diminish late in training, suggesting SEM stabilizes learning dynamics rather than fundamentally improving asymptotic performance

Insufficient comparison to alternatives: Fig. 7 compares only to old baselines (C-RELU, Gumbel+ST, VQ); missing comparisons to SimBaV2 (used as baseline), recent representation regularization methods (DR3, orthogonality), and sparsity work cited in paper

Unresolved hyperparameter sensitivity: paper uses fixed L, V, τ across experiments despite acknowledging RL sensitivity; ablations show these matter significantly but provide no principled selection method; V=64 highlighted without justification

Limited insight into when/why SEM helps: no characterization of failure modes; post-hoc explanations for why actor > critic without original contribution; unclear domain/algorithm dependence; no guidance for practitioners on applicability

Questionable design choices: CIFAR-10 experiment feels disconnected from RL setup; comparison to FastTD3 (speed-optimized) on sample efficiency is somewhat unfair; penultimate layer placement lacks ablation justifying position choice

Methodological concerns: deprecated IsaacGym simulator reduces reproducibility; code not provided; baseline hyperparameter tuning not fully detailed; no statistical significance testing; improvements often within baseline variance

strengths: Clear problem motivation linking non-stationarity to representation collapse in deep RL
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse algorithms (FastTD3, FastSAC, PPO) and environments (28 HumanoidBench, 9 IsaacGym, 27 Atari, MTBench, real robot)
Thorough mechanistic analysis with multiple representation diagnostics (effective rank, dormant neurons, TD error, critic disagreement) connecting empirical gains to theory
Practical value: consistent sample efficiency improvements without wall-clock overhead; algorithm-agnostic and easy to integrate
Excellent reproducibility with extensive hyperparameter tables, architecture details, and per-task learning curves across all domains
Well-executed ablations on SEM parameters (L, V, τ) and comparisons to alternative discretization methods (C-ReLU, Gumbel+ST, VQ)
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: SEM is from Lavoie et al. (2023); contribution is primarily application to RL rather than methodological innovation

Weak theoretical justification: Theorem 1 straightforwardly shows drift causes dormancy but doesn't analyze SEM's solution; no sample complexity bounds or convergence analysis; missing rigorous explanation for why simplicial structure specifically helps RL

Incomplete non-stationarity analysis: CIFAR-10 label-shuffling experiment is artificial compared to actual policy-driven distribution shift; formal theory doesn't explain how SEM prevents identified pathologies

Hyperparameter guidance lacking: SEM introduces L, V, τ but paper provides only heuristics (Fig. 7) without principled selection procedure; contradicts acknowledgment of RL's hyperparameter sensitivity

Limited failure mode characterization: paper claims SEM is 'not universal' for extreme shift/sparse rewards but provides no empirical demonstration; untested on vision-conditioned and language-conditioned RL
Modest empirical gains in many tasks (~20-30% sample efficiency improvement); some learning curves in Appendix show substantial overlap between baseline and SEM
Wall-clock overhead claim slightly overstated: Table 2 shows a few tasks with SEM slower (e.g., h1hand-walk +11 min, h1hand-stair +4 min)
Mechanistic arguments could be stronger: Fig. 4 shows increased effective rank but doesn't establish causality; is higher Gini sparsity a cause or consequence of better performance?

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Non-stationarity leading to representation collapse is well-illustrated via CIFAR-10 experiment with dormant neurons and reduced effective rank

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: Multiple algorithms (FastTD3, FastTD3-SimBaV2, FastSAC, PPO) across diverse benchmarks (28+ HumanoidBench tasks, Isaac Gym, Atari-28, MTBench, real robot), with proper experimental methodology (6 seeds for continuous, confidence intervals)

Detailed mechanistic analysis: Goes beyond returns to analyze learning dynamics (TD error, critic disagreement) and representation quality (effective rank, sparsity, entropy), clearly connecting improvements to underlying mechanisms
Practical advantages: Zero computational overhead, no auxiliary losses, easy integration into existing code—significant advantage over representation methods like SPR
Extensive baseline comparisons: Thorough evaluation against 11+ alternative methods (Regen, Spectral Norm, MoEs, Dropout, etc.) in appendices, providing comprehensive contextualization
Consistent improvements across diverse settings: While often modest, improvements appear reliable across multiple algorithms and benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution is applying existing SEM technique (Lavoie et al., 2023) to deep RL without methodological or theoretical innovations specific to RL. This is primarily an engineering validation rather than advancing the field's understanding

Modest empirical gains: Improvements are often marginal—asymptotic returns on HumanoidBench frequently converge to baseline levels, Atari gains appear minimal, and improvements sometimes fall within confidence intervals suggesting potential lack of statistical significance

Fails on value-based RL: SEM provides no consistent improvements on PQN (Appendix M, Figure 38), contradicting broad applicability claims. Paper acknowledges this but offers no explanation, indicating incomplete understanding

Shallow theoretical understanding: Theorem 1 is standard (relating tracking error to neuron dormancy). The paper doesn't explain why simplex constraints specifically solve this—why not other bounded/sparse representations? Jump from CIFAR-10 motivation (shuffled labels) to RL (policy drift) lacks rigorous justification

Hyperparameter tuning required: SEM introduces hyperparameters (L, V, τ) needing tuning. Different benchmarks use different values (L=2,V=64 vs L=128,V=4) without principled selection guidance. Claims of 'lightweight' somewhat undermined
Incomplete failure analysis: Beyond PQN, the paper doesn't characterize when/why SEM helps or fails. Which task properties determine effectiveness? No systematic investigation of SEM's scope

Incomplete comparisons: Limited engagement with concurrent work addressing similar stability issues (SimBaV2, Lee et al. 2025b). Comparisons to other geometric constraints or structured representations mostly in appendices
Limited domain coverage: Primarily humanoid and Atari. No evaluation on sparse reward RL, vision-based RL with real images, language-conditioned tasks, or systematic exploration of domain boundaries
Experimental design concern: Uses default hyperparameters for baselines but not optimized versions. Paper acknowledges RL sensitivity to hyperparameters but doesn't address this for fair comparison
Dense presentation: 46-page paper; key results relegated to appendices. Theorem 1 mechanism for why SEM helps could be deeper
